---
<!-- theorema-1: body_md -->
Let $J$ be a combinatorial regular $\mathcal{D}$-class of a finite semigroup, with structure matrix $R$. Then $J$ has a permutation matching if and only if $R$ admits a balanced weighting.
<!-- end theorema-1 -->
<!-- theoremb-1: body_md -->
For every $n \ge 1$, the monoid $\mathcal{O}_n$ has a permutation matching.
<!-- end theoremb-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:crossed}
The \emph{crossed square} of $R$ is the relation $\Gamma(R)$ on $P \times Q$ given by
\[
\Gamma(R) \;=\; \bigl\{\, \bigl((A,B),(C,D)\bigr) \;:\; (A,D) \in R \ \text{ and } \ (C,B) \in R \,\bigr\} .
\]
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:weighting}
A \emph{balanced weighting} of $R$ is a function $w : P \times Q \to [0,\infty)$ vanishing off $R$ for which there are constants $a,b>0$ with
\[
\sum_{D \in Q} w(A,D) = a \quad (A \in P), \qquad \sum_{A \in P} w(A,D) = b \quad (D \in Q).
\]
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:birkhoff}
Every doubly stochastic matrix is a convex linear combination of permutation matrices: if $M$ is doubly stochastic then $M = \sum_{k} \lambda_k P_k$ for some permutation matrices $P_k$ and reals $\lambda_k > 0$ with $\sum_k \lambda_k = 1$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:support}
Let $V$ be a finite set and $N \subseteq V \times V$. If there is a doubly stochastic matrix $M$, with rows and columns indexed by $V$, whose entry $M(u,v)$ is non-zero only when $(u,v) \in N$, then some permutation of $V$ is contained in $N$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Write $M = \sum_k \lambda_k P_k$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:birkhoff}, fix any $k$, and let $\sigma$ be the permutation with matrix $P_k$. For each $u$ the entry of $P_k$ at $(u,\sigma(u))$ is $1$, and all terms of the sum are non-negative, so $M(u,\sigma(u)) \ge \lambda_k > 0$. Hence $(u,\sigma(u)) \in N$ for every $u$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:crossed}
If $R$ admits a balanced weighting, then some permutation of $P \times Q$ is contained in $\Gamma(R)$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $w$ be a balanced weighting with constants $a,b$ and set, for $u = (A,B)$ and $v = (C,D)$,
\[
M(u,v): \;=\; \frac{w(A,D)\,w(C,B)}{ab} \;\ge\; 0 .
\]
The sum over the row indexed by $u$ factorises because the summation indices $C$ and $D$ occur in separate factors, and so:
\[
\sum_{(C,D)} M(u,v) \;=\; \frac{1}{ab}\Bigl(\sum_{D} w(A,D)\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{C} w(C,B)\Bigr) \;=\; \frac{a\,b}{ab} \;=\; 1 ,
\]
by the row condition of Definition~\ref{def:weighting} for the sum over $D$ and the column condition for the sum over $C$. Dually each column sum is $\tfrac{1}{ab}\cdot b\cdot a = 1$, so $M$ is doubly stochastic. If $M(u,v) > 0$ then $w(A,D)>0$ and $w(C,B)>0$, so $(A,D) \in R$ and $(C,B) \in R$, that is $(u,v) \in \Gamma(R)$. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:support} now gives the result.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:converse}
If some permutation of $P \times Q$ is contained in $\Gamma(R)$, then $R$ admits a balanced weighting, with constants $a = |Q|$ and $b = |P|$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $\sigma$ be such a permutation and write $\sigma(A,B) = \bigl(C(A,B),\, D(A,B)\bigr)$. Define
\[
w(A,D) \;=\; \bigl|\{\, B \in Q \;:\; D(A,B) = D \,\}\bigr| .
\]
If $w(A,D) > 0$ then $D = D(A,B)$ for some $B$, and $\bigl((A,B),\sigma(A,B)\bigr) \in \Gamma(R)$ gives $(A,D) \in R$; so $w$ vanishes off $R$.

Fix $A \in P$. Every $B \in Q$ satisfies $D(A,B) = D$ for exactly one $D \in Q$, so the $|Q|$ elements $B$ are distributed among the values $w(A,D)$, whence $\sum_{D} w(A,D) = |Q|$.

Fix $D \in Q$. Then
\[
\sum_{A \in P} w(A,D) \;=\; \bigl|\{\, u \in P\times Q : D(u) = D \,\}\bigr| \;=\; \bigl|\sigma^{-1}\bigl(P \times \{D\}\bigr)\bigr| \;=\; \bigl|P \times \{D\}\bigr| \;=\; |P| ,
\]
the third equality because $\sigma$ is a bijection. Therefore $w$ is a balanced weighting with $a = |Q|$ and $b = |P|$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
$\Rightarrow)$ For $x=(A,B) \in J$, $y=(C,D)$ is an inverse of $x$ if and only if $\bigl((A,B),(C,D)\bigr) \in \Gamma(R)$, \cite[Theorem 2.3.4]{Howie}. Hence the given permutation matching of $J$ is contained in  $\Gamma(R)$, and so by Proposition ~\ref{prop:converse}, $R$ admits a balanced weighting with constants $a = |Q|$ and $b = |P|$. 

$\Leftarrow)$ Conversely, given a balanced weighting of $R$, by Proposition \ref{prop:crossed}, $\Gamma (R)$ contains a  permutation, which is the required matching for $J$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:assemble}
A finite regular semigroup $S$ has a permutation matching if and only if the
structure matrix of each $0$-rectangular band $(D_x \cup \{0\})/\mathcal{H}$
admits a balanced weighting.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By \cite[Theorem 1.6]{H14}, $S$ has a permutation matching if and only if each $0$-rectangular band $(D_x \cup \{0\})/\mathcal{H}$ has a permutation matching, whence the result follows from Theorem A.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:criterion}
Let $P$ and $Q$ be finite non-empty sets and $R \subseteq P \times Q$. Then $R$ admits a
balanced weighting if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:crit}
|Q|\,|X| \;\le\; |P|\,|R(X)| \qquad \text{for every } X \subseteq P .
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Write $p = |P|$ and $q = |Q|$. We may normalise the constants of Definition 2.2: if $w$ is a balanced weighting with constants $a$ and $b$ then, since $ap = bq$, the weighting
$(q/a)\,w$ has row sums $q$ and column sums $p$. And so throughout we take
\begin{equation}\label{eq:norm}
\sum_{D \in Q} w(A,D) = q \quad (A \in P), \qquad
\sum_{A \in P} w(A,D) = p \quad (D \in Q),
\end{equation}
and note that the total weight is then $pq$, counted either way.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Necessity.} Let $w$ satisfy \eqref{eq:norm} and let $X \subseteq P$. Summing
the row conditions over $X$ gives $\sum_{A \in X}\sum_{D \in Q} w(A,D) = |X|\,q$. Every
non-zero term of that double sum has $(A,D) \in R$ with $A \in X$, hence $D \in R(X)$; so
the sum is at most $\sum_{D \in R(X)}\sum_{A \in P} w(A,D) = p\,|R(X)|$, which is
\eqref{eq:crit}.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Sufficiency.} Assume \eqref{eq:crit} and build a network $\mathcal{N}$ as
follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item Vertices: a source $\sigma$, a sink $\tau$, a vertex $u_A$ for each $A \in P$, and a vertex $v_D$ for each $D \in Q$.
\item Arcs $\sigma \to u_A$ of capacity $q$, one for each $A \in P$.
\item Arcs $u_A \to v_D$ of capacity $\infty$, one for each pair $(A,D) \in R$ and no others.
\item Arcs $v_D \to \tau$ of capacity $p$, one for each $D \in Q$.
\end{itemize}

The dictionary between $\mathcal{N}$ and the objects of the theorem is this. The vertices
$u_A$ correspond to the elements of $P$, that is to the rows of $R$, and the vertices $v_D$ to the elements of $Q$, its columns;
the middle arcs are exactly the cells of $R$, so an assignment of values to them is exactly a function vanishing off $R$; the capacity $q$ on $\sigma \to u_A$ is the required row sum of $w$ and the capacity
$p$ on $v_D \to \tau$ its required column sum. Precisely: given a flow $f$ of value $pq$,
put $w(A,D) = f(u_A \to v_D)$ for $(A,D) \in R$ and $w(A,D) = 0$ otherwise. The total
capacity leaving $\sigma$ is $pq$ and the total capacity entering $\tau$ is $pq$, so a flow
of value $pq$ saturates every arc at $\sigma$ and every arc at $\tau$. Conservation at
$u_A$ then reads $\sum_D w(A,D) = q$ and conservation at $v_D$ reads $\sum_A w(A,D) = p$,
which is \eqref{eq:norm}. Conversely a $w$ satisfying \eqref{eq:norm} defines in the same way a flow of value $pq$. So it suffices to produce a flow of value $pq$. 

No flow has value exceeding $pq$, the capacity of the cut $\{\sigma\}$; so the theorem applies, and it is enough to show that every cut has capacity at least $pq$.

Let $S$ be a cut and put $X = \{A \in P : u_A \in S\}$ and $Y = \{D \in Q : v_D \in S\}$.
If some $A \in X$ had a $D \in N(A)$ with $D \notin Y$, the arc $u_A \to v_D$ would run
from $S$ to its complement and the cut would have infinite capacity; so we may assume
$R(X) \subseteq Y$. The arcs leaving $S$ are then precisely the arcs $\sigma \to u_A$ with
$A \notin X$, of total capacity $q\,(p - |X|)$, together with the arcs $v_D \to \tau$ with
$D \in Y$, of total capacity $p\,|Y|$. Hence, using $R(X) \subseteq Y$ and then
\eqref{eq:crit},
\[
c(S) \;=\; q\,\bigl(p - |X|\bigr) + p\,|Y| \;\ge\; pq - q|X| + p\,|R(X)| \;\ge\; pq .
\]
Every cut therefore has capacity at least $pq$, so the maximum flow has value $pq$ and the
required weighting exists.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:fail}
The hypothesis of Theorem~A can fail. Let $P = \{p_1,p_2,p_3\}$, $Q = \{q_1,q_2\}$ and $R = \{(p_1,q_2),(p_2,q_2),(p_3,q_1)\}$, which has no empty row or column and so represents the structure matrix of a $0$-rectangular band (this is essentially \cite[Example 1.3]{H14}). The elements $(p_1,q_1)$ and $(p_2,q_1)$ of $P \times Q$ are each related in $\Gamma(R)$ only to $(p_3,q_2)$, since $M(q_1) = \{p_3\}$ and
$N(p_1) = N(p_2) = \{q_2\}$. Therefore no permutation is contained in $\Gamma(R)$, and the $\mathcal{D}$-class has no permutation matching.  Taking $X = \{p_1,p_2\}$ gives $R(X) = \{q_2\}$ and so
\[
|Q|\,|X| = 2\times 2 =  4 \;>\; 3 = 3 \times 1 = |P|\,|R(X)| ,
\] violating the inequality (1), in accord with Theorem \ref{thm:criterion}.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
For $A \in P_r$ and $D = \{d_1 < \cdots < d_r\} \in Q_r$, we say that $D$ is a \emph{transversal} of $A$, written $A \mathrel{R} D$, if $d_i \in A_i$ for every $i$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
{\label{rem:trans}}
The structure matrix $R$ of $D_r$ is defined by the transversal relation in that $(A,B)$ represents an idempotent exactly when $A \mathrel{R} B$; this is because a map of rank $r$ is idempotent, and so generates a $1$ at position $(A,B)$, precisely when it fixes each of the $r$ members of its image, that is when $b_i \in A_i$ for every $i$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:enc}
Let $A \in P_r$ have cut points $a_1 < \cdots < a_{r-1}$ and let $D = \{d_1<\cdots<d_r\} \in Q_r$. Put
\[
s(A) = \bigl(a_1-1,\ \dots,\ a_{r-1}-(r-1)\bigr), \qquad t(D) = \bigl(d_1-1,\ \dots,\ d_r-r\bigr).
\]
Then $s : P_r \to M_{r-1}$ and $t : Q_r \to M_r$ are bijections, with $|M_{r-1}| = \binom{n-1}{r-1}$ and $|M_r| = \binom{n}{r}$; and, writing $s(A) = (s_1,\dots,s_{r-1})$ and $t(D) = (t_1,\dots,t_r)$,
\[
A \mathrel{R} D \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad t_1 \le s_1 \le t_2 \le s_2 \le \cdots \le s_{r-1} \le t_r .
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The cut points of members of $P_r$ are exactly the sequences $1 \le a_1 < \cdots < a_{r-1} \le n-1$. Subtracting $i$ from $a_i$ converts strict increase into weak increase and is invertible, the bounds becoming $0 \le s_1$ and $s_{r-1} \le (n-1)-(r-1) = n-r$; so $s$ is a bijection onto $M_{r-1}$, of size $\binom{m+r-2}{r-1} = \binom{n-1}{r-1}$ as $m+r-2 = n-1$. In the same way $1 \le d_1 < \cdots < d_r \le n$ corresponds to $0 \le t_1 \le \cdots \le t_r \le n-r$, and $|M_r| = \binom{m+r-1}{r} = \binom{n}{r}$.

For the last part, $A \mathrel{R} D$ says $a_{i-1} < d_i \le a_i$ for $i = 1,\dots,r$. The extreme constraints $0 < d_1$ and $d_r \le n$ hold automatically. For $1 \le i \le r-1$, the condition $d_i \le a_i$ reads $t_i + i \le s_i + i$, that is $t_i \le s_i$; and $a_i < d_{i+1}$ reads $s_i + i < t_{i+1}+i+1$, that is $s_i \le t_{i+1}$. Together these give the displayed chain.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
The \emph{deletion incidence} is $e : M_{r-1}\times M_r \to \mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$,
\[
e(s,t) \;=\; \#\bigl\{\, i \in \{1,\dots,r\} \;:\; t \text{ with its } i\text{-th entry deleted equals } s \,\bigr\} .
\]
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:del}
For all $s \in M_{r-1}$ and $t \in M_r$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item if $e(s,t)>0$ then $s$ and $t$ interlace, in the sense of Lemma~\ref{lem:enc};
\item $\sum_{s \in M_{r-1}} e(s,t) = r$ for every $t \in M_r$;
\item $\sum_{t \in M_r} e(s,t) = n$ for every $s \in M_{r-1}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
(1) Write $t = (t_1 \le \cdots \le t_r)$ and let $s = (s_1 \le \cdots \le s_{r-1})$ arise by deleting the $i$-th entry, so $s_j = t_j$ for $j<i$ and $s_j = t_{j+1}$ for $j \ge i$. We check $t_j \le s_j \le t_{j+1}$ for $1 \le j \le r-1$. If $j<i$ then $t_j \le s_j$ holds with equality, while $s_j = t_j \le t_{j+1}$ as $t$ is weakly increasing. If $j \ge i$ then $t_j \le t_{j+1} = s_j$ as $t$ is weakly increasing, while $s_j \le t_{j+1}$ holds with equality.

(2) Deleting any one of the $r$ entries of $t$ leaves some member of $M_{r-1}$, so the sum counts the positions of $t$.

(3) Fix $s$, so $\sum_{v\in\Sigma} |s|_v = r-1$. A multiset $t$ contributes only if deleting some entry of $t$ leaves $s$, hence only if $t = s \uplus \{v\}$ for some $v \in \Sigma$; distinct $v$ give distinct $t$, so these contributions do not overlap. For $t = s\uplus\{v\}$ the positions whose deletion leaves $s$ are exactly those carrying the value $v$, of which there are $|s|_v + 1$. Hence
\[
\sum_{t \in M_r} e(s,t) \;=\; \sum_{v\in\Sigma}\bigl(|s|_v  + 1\bigr) \;=\; (r-1)+|\Sigma| \;=\; (r-1)+(n-r+1) \;=\; n ,
\]
which does not depend on $s$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
When $n=3$, $r=2$ we have $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$, and $e$ is the following
array, with rows indexed by $M_{r-1} = \{(0),(1)\}$ and columns by
$M_r = \{(0,0),(0,1),(1,1)\}$, margins shown:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc|c}
      & (0,0) & (0,1) & (1,1) & \\\hline
(0)   & 2     & 1     & 0     & 3\\
(1)   & 0     & 1     & 2     & 3\\\hline
      & 2     & 2     & 2     &
\end{array}
\]
The two zeros in the array indicate where pairs fail to interlace: deleting an entry of $(1,1)$ yields $(1)$, never $(0)$, and similarly deleting from $(0,0)$ cannot yield a $(1)$.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:weighting}
For each $r$ the transversal relation $R \subseteq P_r \times Q_r$ admits the balanced weighting $w_r(A,D) = e\bigl(s(A),t(D)\bigr)$, with constants $a = n$ and $b = r$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:del}(1) with Lemma~\ref{lem:enc}, $w_r$ vanishes off $R$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:del}(3) each row sum is $n$ and by Lemma~\ref{lem:del}(2) each column sum is $r$, the bijections of Lemma~\ref{lem:enc} matching the index sets.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By Corollary 3.6 the structure matrix of $D_r$, which by Definition 3.1 and Remark~\ref{rem:trans} is the transversal relation $R \subseteq P_r \times Q_r$,
admits a balanced weighting. Hence by Theorem~A each $D_r$ has a permutation
matching, and since the inverses of any element lie in its own
$\mathcal{D}$-class, these combine to give a permutation matching of
$\mathcal{O}_n$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
